Based on genetic similarity to reference populations, 69.0% of participants aligned with European, 18.5% with African, 10.0% with Admixed American, and approximately 1% or fewer aligned with East Asian, Middle Eastern, or South Asian genetic ancestry (34).

PRS and SDoH associate with disease

The number of prevalent cases ranged from 1,098 for T1D to 17,747 for T2D (Supplementary Table 6). In the overall AoU study cohort, each PRS, which was mean-and variance-normalized using genetic principal components (PCs), was significantly associated with AoU case status after adjustment for sex/gender, age, age², visit frequency, and record depth (Figure 1; top row). Effect sizes varied across diseases, ranging from 1.25 times the odds of asthma to 1.85 times the odds of T2D per one standard deviation (SD) increase in PRS (Supplementary Table 10). Of the 72 disease-SDoH pairs tested, 64 exhibited significant associations between SDoH and AoU case status after Bonferroni correction (P < 6.25 × 10 ).

The direction of association was generally consistent across non-cancer diseases, with greater individual-level social vulnerability associated with higher odds of disease. In contrast, greater individual-level social vulnerability was associated with lower odds of breast and prostate cancer, potentially reflecting differences in disease ascertainment across social contexts (44). Notably, the association between individual-level education and disease was comparable in magnitude to that of PRS for T2D, CKD, and T1D, while associations with individual-level poverty were sometimes even larger. Adjustment for 16 genetic PCs as covariates attenuated some associations, which may reflect residual confounding by population structure (even with PRS whose means and variances were already adjusted for PCs) as well as shared variation between genetic ancestry and social context (Supplementary Figure 9).

Genetic effect modification

To investigate whether the association between PRS and disease varies across levels of social vulnerability, we compared PRS-disease associations between individuals in the highest and lowest quintiles (Q1 vs Q5) of nine SDoH measures (Supplementary Table 8). We observed consistent evidence of effect modification for multiple cardiometabolic diseases, including T2D, CKD, and CHD, with PRS ORs differing significantly between SDoH extremes for most SDoH measures (Bonferroni-adjusted z test, P < 6.94 × 10 ) (Figure 2, Supplementary Table 11). For example, each one SD increase in PRS was associated with 2.15 [95% CI: 2.03, 2.27] times the odds of T2D in the lowest individual-level poverty quintile, compared with 1.58 [1.51, 1.65] times the odds in the highest poverty quintile (P=8.28 × 10 ¹ for the difference between quintiles). All non-cancer diseases exhibited evidence of effect modification by individual-level poverty. The association for Afib was only nominally significant, which may reflect the smaller number of cases and controls available for that analysis or the overall relatively weaker PRS association (OR 1.32) in this cohort. Across SDoH-trait pairs with significant effect modification, the relative effect of PRS on disease was always stronger in groups experiencing lower social vulnerability. Further reinforcing these findings, 18 of 19 SDoH-trait pairs (94.7%) that exhibited statistically significant differences in PRS ORs between SDoH extremes also had significant PRS x SDoH interaction terms in a whole population analysis not limited to SDoH extremes, with three additional pairs reaching significance (Supplementary Figure 10, Supplementary Table 12).

Due to the complex population structure of the AoU cohort and reduced PRS accuracy in non-EUR genetic similarity groups (45), residual confounding may influence these findings if genetic ancestry proportions differ across SDoH strata, potentially contributing to differences in observed PRS-disease associations (Supplementary Figure 4). Therefore, to further assess potential confounding by population structure, we performed two sensitivity analyses. Additional inclusion of PCs as covariates led to largely consistent results (Supplementary Figure 11; Supplementary Table 13). We also repeated analyses within the two largest genetic similarity clusters (Supplementary Figure 12; Supplementary Table 14). Although this attenuated associations, a comparable loss of significance was observed in randomly downsampled wholepopulation analyses, suggesting that the reduction was largely attributable to decreased sample size rather than residual confounding by ancestry, though such tests should be repeated as sample sizes increase (Supplementary Figure 13; Supplementary Table 15). Therefore, we concluded that our results are likely not due to residual confounding by genetic substructure as captured by the PCs. AoU also contains more comprehensive individual-level SDoH data derived from the SDoH and Healthcare Access and Utilization (HCAU) surveys. These measures were not included in the main analysis as requiring survey completion substantially reduced sample size and generalizability due to nonrandom response patterns that favor older, White participants with higher income and educational attainment, as described previously (Supplementary Table 5) (38, 40). As such, these analyses are considered exploratory. To account for reduced sample size, this analysis was restricted to diseases with more than 3,000 cases among participants with available survey data (Afib, T2D, CKD, CHD, and asthma) (Supplementary Table 9). Even after controlling for individual-level poverty and education, we observed significant effect modification of the PRS by other SDoH factors following FDR correction, including food insecurity for Afib, CHD, and asthma; low social cohesion among neighbors for CHD; uninsured status for Afib and CKD; perceived neighborhood crime for CHD, and non-homeownership for Afib, T2D, CKD, and CHD (Figure 3; Supplementary Table 16). An additional fourteen pairs showed nominal significance (Supplementary Figure 14). Consistent with our primary analyses, PRS explained more variability in disease among socially advantaged groups across each SDoH domain. After additionally controlling for 16 genetic PCs as covariates, only food insecurity and perceived neighborhood crime remained associated with significant effect modification of the Afib and CHD PRSs (Supplementary Figure 15, Supplementary Table 17). To better visualize the practical implications of these effect modifications, we plotted the conditional effects of PRS for an average individual at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of social vulnerability (Figure 4; Supplementary Figure 16). As expected, the predicted case probabilities increase with increasing PRS (Figure 4, x axis). Across diseases, predicted case probabilities are also higher among groups experiencing greater social vulnerability, particularly at lower levels of genetic risk (Figure 4, yellow > grey > blue lines). Across SDoH, we observe non-parallel/converging slopes, consistent with gene-environment interactions, wherein those with low genetic risk experience more variability in AoU case status by social environment. Alternatively, genetic risk has a greater effect on disease when social vulnerability is low (Supplementary Figure 17). For example, a one SD increase in PRS within participants at the associated with disease odds for four out of six of the remaining diseases under the fixedeffects meta-analysis framework, indicating significant transferability (Supplementary Figure 27; Supplementary Table 32). Additionally, CHD and T2D PsRS were significant under the randomeffects framework and showed the strongest transferability. For T2D, the random-effects metaanalysis estimated an OR of 1.50 [95% CI: 1.21, 1.85] per one SD increase in PsRS, compared with an OR of 2.01 [95% CI: 1.96, 2.05] in the AoU training cohort under the five-fold crossvalidation framework, while the CHD PsRS demonstrated a similar association in the external and AoU cohorts. PRS were more consistently and more strongly associated with disease in external testing cohorts (Figure 7). This was not always the case in AoU, indicating some overfitting of the PsRS AoU model. In MGBB, joint modeling PsRS alongside PRS and base covariates resulted in a statistically significant increase in AUC compared to the genetic model for every disease except asthma (Supplementary Figure 28; Supplementary Tables 33 34). Further demonstrating generalizability, PsRS trained in MGBB or PEGS performed similarly to those trained in AoU within their respective cohorts, although breast and prostate cancer sample sizes in PEGS were too small to train PsRS (Supplementary Figure 29).

Discussion

We leveraged SDoH, genetic, and EHR data from the large, diverse AoU dataset to identify genetic effect modification by SDoH across multiple cardiometabolic diseases and develop transferable PsRS. When evaluating PRS associations for eight chronic diseases prioritized for clinical implementation, we found evidence of significant genetic effect modification by SDoH. PRS associations with cardiometabolic diseases were attenuated in socially vulnerable populations; social factors had a larger effect on AoU case status among individuals with lower genetic risk and a lesser effect among high genetic risk individuals. Nevertheless, social risk explained substantial case variation among individuals even in the highest decile of predicted genetic risk. Encouragingly, joint modeling of social risk, in the form of PsRS, alongside PRS significantly improved disease prediction for all eight diseases. Moreover, four out of six of the PsRS trained in AoU showed transferability in external datasets. Together these results highlight the power and utility of incorporating SDoH into disease prediction models alongside PRS. In models stratified into top and bottom SDoH quintiles, we saw evidence of genetic effect modification by both individual and area-level SDoH for T2D, CKD, and CHD PRS, and by individual poverty for asthma and T1D PRS. Notably, PRSs with significant effect modification were those which had the strongest residual correlation with SDoH after PC mean and variance adjustment; however, the persistence of interaction effects after more extensive PC adjustment (additionally including PCs as covariates) indicates that these findings likely reflect, at least in part, genuine heterogeneity in PRS associations across social environments. This is further supported by PRS effect modification by SES in European-ancestry-only cohorts (47). Moreover, all diseases with sufficient sample sizes to evaluate the more comprehensive individual-level survey measures (asthma, Afib, T2D CKD, and CHD), displayed effect modification by at least one other SDoH variable following FDR correction, even after controlling for individual poverty and education. While the SDoH survey-based analyses should be considered exploratory until these measures are more broadly collected in diverse populations (38), the findings suggest that individual-level SDoH beyond more commonly reported income and education SES metrics, for example healthcare coverage and home ownership, may be important to consider when evaluating PRS transferability and equitable clinical implementation. For SDoH-trait pairs with significant differences in PRS odds ratios between the most and least socially advantaged groups, PRS consistently had a stronger association in the socially advantaged population, suggesting that environmental factors may contribute to lack of PRS transferability across populations with different social exposures (8, 9, 48). Negative interaction terms and conditional effect analyses indicated that SDoH had a stronger association with AoU case status among individuals with low genetic risk. In other words, as genetic risk increased, the association between social vulnerability and disease was attenuated; likewise, as social vulnerability increased, the predictive contribution of genetics was attenuated. One possible explanation is that when social factors account for a greater proportion of variation in disease risk, PRS may explain a smaller proportion of the remaining variation in disease risk (8, 9, 48). This attenuation may also partly reflect differences in disease prevalence across social strata: when socially vulnerable groups have a higher underlying disease prevalence, a similar increment in genetic liability may correspond to a smaller relative increase in prevalence, resulting in an apparently weaker PRS effect on the multiplicative scale (47). An alternative explanation is that PRS are less predictive in socially disadvantaged populations due to their underrepresentation in Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS) training data, although SNP effect sizes have been found to be relatively stable across environmental strata and generally each SNP explains a small portion of trait variance (30, 49). Considering SDoH, in the form of PsRS, alongside genetic risk improved disease prediction for all eight chronic diseases tested here. To evaluate their generalizability, we validated the PsRS in two independent cohorts, MGBB and PEGS, where they demonstrated moderate transferability. While PRS had stronger effects than PsRS in these cohorts, the PRS had more predictors and were trained on larger sample sizes than AoU alone. Moreover, each external cohort presented distinct limitations for PsRS construction (absence of income data in MGBB, small sample size in PEGS). Despite these limitations, fixed-effects meta-analyses of AoUtrained PsRS were significantly associated with disease odds for four of the six diseases, and T2D and CHD PsRS demonstrated the greatest transferability. This study has several strengths. First, AoU is one of the largest and most diverse biomedical datasets and is among the first to collect genomic data, EHRs, and rich individual-level and area-level SDoH data. Second, we focused on clinically relevant chronic diseases and corresponding PRS already developed and validated by eMERGE, increasing translational relevance. Third, to our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to systematically evaluate interactions between PRS and SDoH across multiple chronic diseases within a single cohort, improving comparability across diseases and demonstrating the potential generality of these effects. Methodologically, we supported our findings using multiple complementary approaches-combining stratified analyses with formal interaction models-and ran sensitivity analyses to help address potential confounding from population stratification. We further extended prior work by incorporating a broader and more granular set of SDoH measures than is typical in PRS studies, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of social context. Finally, we developed PsRS that leverage the scale and diversity of AoU, and demonstrated their ability to improve disease prediction across a range of diseases and their transferability in external cohorts, supporting their potential real-world applicability in diverse healthcare settings. This study also has some limitations. First, EHR completeness and depth, and SDoH survey data are subject to selection and data availability bias influenced by demographic, socioeconomic, and health care access factors ( (38, 40)). EHR-derived phenotypes are affected by clinical ascertainment, including screening intensity (e.g., for breast and prostate cancer), which may introduce residual confounding when interpreting gene-environment interaction effects. Second, detecting interaction effects typically requires substantially larger sample sizes than main effects. Accordingly, the presence of effect modification in higher-powered diseases and the absence of detectable interactions in others may partly reflect limited statistical power rather than true absence of effect modification. Third, PRS may capture population-stratificationrelated signal, particularly when genetic ancestry is correlated with social and environmental variables and when genome-wide construction methods are used (50). The eMERGE-selected PRS used in this study included both genome-wide (asthma, CKD, CHD, T2D) and sparse scores (breast cancer, prostate cancer, afib, T1D), potentially contributing to heterogeneity in the extent of population-stratification-related confounding across diseases. Due to the correlation between genetic PCs and social and environmental variables, adjustment for genetic PCs to reduce confounding from population stratification may also attenuate some true SDoHrelated signal, thus providing a conservative estimate of interaction effects. Finally, the external validation results likely represent conservative estimates of PsRS performance due to the lack of individual-level poverty data in MGBB and the small sample size of the PEGS cohort. As AoU continues to expand and other large-scale datasets increasingly incorporate SDoH measures, these findings should be replicated in independent and more diverse populations, as well as in traditional cohorts or settings with universal healthcare that will be less impacted by and biased according to healthcare access. In addition, as longer follow-up enables greater accrual of incident cases and mortality outcomes, future work should assess effect modification in incident disease contexts and for disease complications. Given known real-world biases in AoU, further studies should also evaluate the extent to which these factors influence the transferability of PsRS, particularly to ensure that they do not reinforce or amplify existing disparities. Moreover, future research should aim to disentangle genetic effect modification due to bias in the training data (for example higher rates of case control misspecification or underrepresentation of socially disadvantaged populations) from true gene-by-environment interactions. Finally, robust incorporation of SDoH into genetic and clinical risk models will require coordinated efforts across biobanks and healthcare systems to improve the collection, harmonization, and analytic integration of social determinants within disease prediction frameworks. This work demonstrates the importance, power, and utility of integrating SDoH into genetic risk prediction models. Failing to account for social context may result in biased disease prediction where disease is underestimated in socially disadvantaged groups due to attenuated genetic effects and omission of key structural determinants of health. Although we focused on eight chronic diseases, complementary work suggests these patterns may generalize across a broader range of PRSs (51). As biomedical research increasingly incorporates social determinants at scale, future research should more systematically investigate these effects and develop robust, transferable social risk models. More broadly, these findings reinforce that personalized medicine requires moving beyond genetic risk alone. Integrating SDoH alongside PRS could offer a more complete and equitable framework for disease risk prediction and clinical implementation. SDoH explain heterogeneity within PRS-defined risk groups

Given that SDoH appeared to exert the greatest influence on AoU case status among individuals with low genetic risk, we next examined the extent to which SDoH explained AoU case status within the lowest genetic risk decile. To this end, and to optimally capture the contributions of both individual-and area-level SDoH, we constructed disease-specific polysocial risk scores (PsRS), in which elastic net models were trained independently on each disease to capture their unique social contributions from the nine different SDoH in the main, larger cohort (Supplementary Figure 8). As expected, we found that PsRS explained a large portion of case heterogeneity in the lowest PRS decile (Supplementary Figure 20; Supplementary Table 20). More relevant to clinical decision-making, PsRS also explained substantial heterogeneity in AoU case status within the highest PRS decile (Figure 5; Supplementary Tables 20 21). For example, among individuals in the top asthma PRS decile, case classification was approximately 30% lower in the lowest PsRS quintile and 50% higher in the highest PsRS quintile relative to the middle quintiles. Net improvement in reclassification showed a 7.4 percentage-point net improvement in continuous risk classification for prostate cancer, and more modest improvements for T2D and asthma (Supplementary Figures 21 22, Supplementary Table 22 23 24 Combining genetic and social risk improves disease prediction modeling across cohorts Next, we were interested in whether jointly modeling genetic and social risk factors could significantly improve disease prediction. While the magnitude of improvement varied, joint modeling PRS and PsRS significantly improved disease prediction for all eight diseases tested here (Figure 6; Supplementary Tables 25 26). For example, including PsRS in the joint model improved T2D AUC from 0.76 for the Genetic model to 0.80 (p<0.00020). Relative to the genetics model, the joint model also shrank the observed/expected ratio closer to 1 across SDoH quintiles for most SDoH-disease pairs and lowered the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for all diseases except Afib and CHD (Supplementary Figures 23 24; Supplementary Tables 27 28). Despite significant interactions between PRS and SDoH with individual measures, including an interaction term between PRS and PsRS did not significantly improve AUC for any condition (Supplementary Figure 25; Supplementary Tables 29). Results remained significant in a sensitivity analysis adjusted for 16 genetic PCs (Supplementary Figure 26, Supplementary Tables 30 31). To evaluate the generalizability of PsRS across healthcare systems and biobanks, we applied PsRS derived from a full-data refit in AoU to the Mass General Brigham Biobank (MGBB) and the Personalized Environment and Gene Study (PEGS).
